name: Silver Ticket STR-169120 Fixed Frame Screen
amazonQuery: Silver Ticket STR-169120 120 inch projector screen
summary: A 120" fixed-frame matte white screen with a velvet-wrapped frame, the long-running value pick for dark home theaters.
verdict:
The Silver Ticket STR-169120 is the screen many first home theaters start with: a **120" 16:9 fixed-frame** screen with a matte white, 4K-rated surface stretched over an aluminum frame wrapped in black velvet. The velvet border soaks up overspill so the image edges look crisp.

Do the brightness maths before you pair it with a projector. A 120" 16:9 screen covers about 42.7 sq ft. With a gain of about **1.1**, a projector rated at 2,800 lumens, such as the [Epson Home Cinema 2350](/gear/epson-home-cinema-2350/), gives roughly 2,800 x 1.1 / 42.7 = **72 foot-lamberts** at its rated output, and a 2,000-lumen projector about 52. Calibrated modes run lower, but both clear the roughly 16 foot-lamberts often cited for SDR cinema with room to spare.

Seating distance follows from the width. The image is 104.6" wide, so a 40-degree viewing angle puts you about **12 ft** back and a 30-degree angle about **16.3 ft** back; try your room with our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/). As a white screen, it has no ambient light rejection, so lights on will gray out blacks. For a light-controlled room it is excellent value; for a living room, look at the [Elite Screens Sable Frame CineGrey 3D](/gear/elite-screens-cinegrey-3d/). More picks in our [best projector screen guide](/best-projector-screen-for-home-theater/).

faqs.q: How far should I sit from a 120-inch Silver Ticket screen?
faqs.a: Roughly 12 to 16 feet. The image is 104.6 inches wide, so a 40-degree viewing angle puts you about 12 feet back and a 30-degree angle about 16.3 feet back. Sit closer for a more cinematic feel, further back for comfort.

faqs.q: Can the Silver Ticket screen be used with an ultra short throw projector?
faqs.a: It is not recommended. Ultra short throw projectors hit the screen at a steep angle, which exaggerates any surface waves and gives no ambient light rejection. Use a ceiling-light-rejecting UST screen instead.

name: Elite Screens Sable Frame 2
summary: A low-cost fixed-frame screen with Elite's 1.1-gain CineWhite material and a velvet frame, a solid match for dark rooms.
verdict:
The Elite Screens Sable Frame 2 is a **fixed-frame, 16:9** screen using Elite's **CineWhite** matte white material, rated at **1.1 gain**, stretched over a black velvet-covered aluminum frame. It is sold in a range of sizes; 120" is the common home theater pick.

The gain number tells you how much light comes back. On a 120" screen (about 42.7 sq ft), a projector rated at 2,300 lumens, like the [BenQ HT2060](/gear/benq-ht2060/), returns roughly 2,300 x 1.1 / 42.7 = **59 foot-lamberts** at its rated output. A 3,000-lumen model such as the [Epson Home Cinema 3800](/gear/epson-home-cinema-3800/) would give about 77. Calibrated output is always lower than the rated figure, but both have headroom in a dark room. A 1.1 gain is close enough to neutral that viewing angles stay wide and even, which matters for a sofa that runs off-center.

What you do not get is ambient light rejection: a white screen reflects room light as readily as projector light, so blacks gray out with lamps on. Assembly is straightforward but best done by two people, and the tension springs need even attention to get a flat surface. If your room is light-controlled, it is one of the best-value screens available; for living rooms, step up to the [Elite Screens Sable Frame CineGrey 3D](/gear/elite-screens-cinegrey-3d/). More in our [best projector screen guide](/best-projector-screen-for-home-theater/).

faqs.q: Is the Elite Sable Frame 2 good for 4K?
faqs.a: Yes. CineWhite is a smooth matte surface suited to 4K projectors, and the fixed frame keeps it flat so fine detail stays sharp.

name: Elite Screens Aeon CLR 3
amazonQuery: Elite Screens Aeon CLR 3 ALR screen
summary: A thin-bezel ceiling-light-rejecting screen built for ultra short throw projectors, the upgrade that makes a UST work in a bright living room.
verdict:
The Elite Screens Aeon CLR 3 is a **ceiling-light-rejecting (CLR) ALR screen** made specifically for **ultra short throw (UST)** projectors. Its surface is engineered to reflect light arriving from below, where a UST sits, back toward the audience, while sending light from the ceiling and above away from your eyes. The edge-free, thin-bezel aluminum frame keeps it looking like a TV on the wall. See [how ALR screens work](/glossary/alr-screen/) for how these screens work.

Why it matters is easy to quantify. A UST like the [Epson EpiqVision Ultra LS800](/gear/epson-ls800/) is rated at 4,000 ISO lumens, which on a 100" screen (29.7 sq ft) is roughly 135 lumens per sq ft at its rated output. Brightness is not the problem in a living room; contrast is. On a white screen, overhead lights add their own reflection to every dark pixel, so blacks turn gray. A CLR surface rejects most of that overhead light, which keeps contrast up even if the screen reflects somewhat less than a 1.0-gain white surface.

The catches: it only works with UST projectors (a ceiling-mounted projector would be rejected like room light), it costs much more than a white screen, and assembly must be careful because any wave shows at UST angles. Pair it with the [Hisense PX3-Pro](/gear/hisense-px3-pro/) or [AWOL Vision LTV-3500 Pro](/gear/awol-ltv-3500-pro/). More options in our [best projector screen guide](/best-projector-screen-for-home-theater/).

faqs.q: Can I use the Elite Aeon CLR 3 with a regular projector?
faqs.a: No. The surface is tuned to reflect light coming from below at a steep angle, as an ultra short throw projector does. Light from a ceiling-mounted or shelf projector is treated like room light and rejected, giving a dim, uneven image.

faqs.q: Do I need a CLR screen for a UST projector?
faqs.a: Not to get a picture, but it makes the biggest difference in bright rooms. A white wall or screen reflects overhead light back at you and grays out blacks. A CLR screen keeps contrast when lights are on, which is how most living rooms are used.

faqs.q: Is the Aeon CLR 3 hard to install?
faqs.a: It takes care rather than skill. Assemble the frame on a clean floor, attach the surface evenly so there are no waves, and level it carefully. Ultra short throw projectors exaggerate any curve or wrinkle in the surface.

name: Elite Screens Spectrum Motorized Screen
amazonQuery: Elite Screens Spectrum electric motorized projector screen 120
summary: An electric motorized drop-down screen with MaxWhite 1.1-gain material and a remote, for rooms where the screen must disappear when not in use.
verdict:
The Elite Screens Spectrum is an **electric motorized** screen that rolls down from a wall- or ceiling-mounted case at the press of a remote, then disappears when the movie ends. It uses Elite's **MaxWhite FG** matte white material at about **1.1 gain**, and a 12-volt trigger input lets compatible projectors lower and raise it automatically.

At 120" 16:9, the image area is about 42.7 sq ft, so the screen returns roughly lumens x 1.1 / 42.7. A 2,600-lumen projector like the [Epson Home Cinema 5050UB](/gear/epson-home-cinema-5050ub/) gives about **67 foot-lamberts** at its rated output; a 3,000-lumen model about 77. That is plenty for a dark room. For seating, the 104.6" image width puts you around **12 ft** back for a 40-degree angle and about 16 ft for 30 degrees; check with our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/).

The trade-off with any roll-down screen is flatness. Without side tensioning, some owners report slight waves or curled edges over time, which show most on bright, flat scenes. That rules it out for ultra short throw projectors, where waves are magnified. There is also no ambient light rejection. If you need a screen that hides away in a living room, it is good value; if it can stay up permanently, a fixed frame like the [Elite Screens Sable Frame 2](/gear/elite-screens-sable-frame-2/) is flatter and cheaper. See our [best projector screen guide](/best-projector-screen-for-home-theater/).

name: Elite Screens Sable Frame CineGrey 3D
summary: A 1.2-gain ambient-light-rejecting fixed-frame screen for standard-throw projectors, the best all-round choice for rooms that are not fully dark.
verdict:
The Elite Screens Sable Frame CineGrey 3D pairs Elite's budget fixed frame with its **CineGrey 3D** ambient-light-rejecting (ALR) material, rated at **1.2 gain**. Unlike a CLR screen for ultra short throw projectors, it is designed for **standard-throw** projectors on a ceiling or rear shelf. See [how ALR screens work](/glossary/alr-screen/) for the difference.

Here is how the gain and grey surface work together. On a 120" screen (42.7 sq ft), a 3,000-lumen projector such as the [Epson Home Cinema 3800](/gear/epson-home-cinema-3800/) returns about 3,000 x 1.2 / 42.7 = **84 foot-lamberts** at its rated output, versus about 70 on a 1.0-gain white screen. The angular-reflective surface sends projector light back toward the seats while reflecting light from other angles away, and the grey base keeps blacks darker when lamps are on. In practice that means a living room with some lights on looks far less washed out than on white.

ALR comes with trade-offs. Viewing angles are narrower than matte white, so very wide seating rows see a dimmer image at the edges, and some viewers notice a faint texture on bright, flat scenes. It is not for UST projectors. For most mixed-use rooms with a standard projector, it is our first choice; for a fully dark theater, the [Elite Screens Sable Frame 2](/gear/elite-screens-sable-frame-2/) is cheaper and just as good. More in our [best projector screen guide](/best-projector-screen-for-home-theater/).

name: VAMVO Ambient Light Rejecting Screen
amazonQuery: VAMVO ALR projector screen fixed frame
summary: A budget fixed-frame ambient-light-rejecting screen; check which version you buy, because UST and standard-throw ALR surfaces are not interchangeable.
verdict:
The VAMVO Ambient Light Rejecting Screen is a budget **fixed-frame ALR** screen sold in several sizes. Its appeal is simple: ALR performance for much less than big-name CLR screens. The thing to get right is the surface type, because ALR screens are built for a specific projector position. See [how ALR screens work](/glossary/alr-screen/).

The geometry is the reason. An **ultra short throw** projector sits below the screen and fires upward at a steep angle, so its screen must reflect light from below and reject light from above. A **standard-throw** projector fires from the ceiling or back of the room, so its ALR screen reflects light from in front. Pair the wrong one and the image looks dim and uneven. Brightness maths still applies: a 3,000-lumen projector on a 100" screen (29.7 sq ft) gives about 101 lumens per sq ft before the screen's gain is applied, so check VAMVO's stated gain for your version and multiply.

Budget ALR materials generally have narrower viewing angles than matte white, and quality control varies more than with established brands, so inspect the surface on arrival. If your budget cannot stretch to the [Elite Screens Aeon CLR 3](/gear/elite-screens-aeon-clr3/) (UST) or [Elite Screens Sable Frame CineGrey 3D](/gear/elite-screens-cinegrey-3d/) (standard throw), it is a reasonable way to add ambient light rejection. Compare in our [best projector screen guide](/best-projector-screen-for-home-theater/).

name: Akia Screens Fixed Frame Screen
amazonQuery: Akia Screens 120 inch fixed frame projector screen
summary: A budget 120" fixed-frame matte white screen that gets you a flat, framed image for little money in a dark room.
verdict:
The Akia Screens Fixed Frame Screen is a **120" 16:9** budget screen with a matte white, 4K-rated surface tensioned over an aluminum frame with a black velvet-style border. It is the cheapest way here to get a flat, framed screen instead of projecting onto a wall.

The maths shows why a real screen beats a painted wall at this price. A 120" image covers about 42.7 sq ft. On a neutral, roughly 1.0-gain white surface, a 3,300-lumen projector like the [Epson Home Cinema 880](/gear/epson-home-cinema-880/) returns about 3,300 / 42.7 = **77 foot-lamberts** at its rated output, and a 2,300-lumen projector about 54. The tensioned surface is also flatter and more uniform than most walls, so there are no texture patterns or color tints. For seating, the 104.6" width works out to about **12 ft** for a 40-degree viewing angle and 16 ft for 30 degrees.

As with any white screen, there is no ambient light rejection, so a dark room is ideal. Frame finish and long-term durability are less proven than Elite or Silver Ticket, and owners note the assembly instructions are basic. If you want a step up in build and consistency, the [Silver Ticket STR-169120 Fixed Frame Screen](/gear/silver-ticket-str-169120/) or [Elite Screens Sable Frame 2](/gear/elite-screens-sable-frame-2/) cost a little more. name: Elite Screens Manual B Pull Down Screen
amazonQuery: Elite Screens Manual B pull down projector screen 100
summary: A simple pull-down screen for rooms where the screen has to disappear, best at 100" in a dark room on a tight budget.
verdict:
The Elite Screens Manual B is a **manual pull-down** screen: you pull it down from a wall- or ceiling-mounted case and it locks in place, then retracts when you are done. It uses a matte white surface of about **1.1 gain** and is commonly bought at **100" 16:9**.

At 100", the image is 87.2" wide and 49" tall, covering about 29.7 sq ft. A 2,000-lumen projector returns roughly 2,000 x 1.1 / 29.7 = **74 foot-lamberts** at its rated output; a budget 3,600-lumen model like the [Optoma HD146X](/gear/optoma-hd146x/) about 133. That is far more than a dark room needs, so a pull-down at this size gives a bright image even from cheap projectors. The 87.2" width puts seating about **10 ft** back for a 40-degree angle and about 13.6 ft for 30 degrees; check with our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/).

The compromise is flatness. Pull-down screens are not tensioned, so slight waves and curled edges are common, especially over time, and they show on bright scenes. That makes it a poor match for ultra short throw projectors and for viewers who notice uniformity issues. There is no ambient light rejection. For a bedroom, rental or multipurpose room on a budget, it does the job; for a permanent theater, a fixed frame like the [Elite Screens Sable Frame 2](/gear/elite-screens-sable-frame-2/) is a clear step up. More in our [best projector screen guide](/best-projector-screen-for-home-theater/).
